title: TestPilot
text: TestPilot. Writes tests, then argues with them. Generates pytest, Jest and JUnit tests and ranks defect-prone files in public GitHub repositories. It retrieves the five most relevant coding-standard chunks first, drafts the tests against them, and an LLM critique loop regenerates anything scoring below 0.6.

title: TestPilot: role and stack
text: Yash's part in TestPilot: Owned everything except the frontend on a four-person team: the AI pipeline, model fine-tuning, defect prediction, CI/CD and the backend. Built with FastAPI, Qwen via Ollama, RAG, pgvector, Random Forest, Docker, Cloud Run. The pipeline runs: Read repository, then Retrieve coding standards, then Draft tests, then Critique gate, then Keep or redraft.

title: CV Studio
text: CV Studio. A résumé editor that compiles real LaTeX. A multi-user workspace where a résumé is edited visually, inspected as LaTeX source, and compiled to PDF on the server with pdflatex (shell escape off, with timeouts). It keeps revision history with restore, rejects silent concurrent overwrites with version checks, and stores job descriptions and text-selection annotations beside each CV.

The pipeline runs: Visual edit, then Generate LaTeX, then Compile with pdflatex, then Protected PDF preview, then Save revision. Links: GitHub: https://github.com/y-bakshi/cv-studio.

title: GuardianAI
text: GuardianAI. Two ways to answer a safety question. A neighborhood safety assistant. Location questions take a 1 to 2 second path through database summaries. Open-ended ones go to a 3 to 4 second ReAct path, so the expensive agent runs only when it is needed. The team later renamed it CityWatch, which is the name its live demo shows. It is a different project from the AWS Ideathon entry below.

title: GuardianAI: role and stack

Built with Next.js, TypeScript, FastAPI, Claude, PostgreSQL, Mapbox, WebSockets. The pipeline runs: Incident map and feeds, then Route the question, then Summary path, then ReAct path, then Safety response. Links: Live demo: https://city-watch-frontend.vercel.app/.

title: Serverless face recognition
text: Serverless face recognition. Detection and recognition as separate stages with a queue between them. MTCNN detection and FaceNet recognition run as separate Lambda functions joined by SQS. Under 100 concurrent requests it reached 99% accuracy at 3.75 seconds average latency, after shrinking a 10 GB container to fit Lambda.

title: TestPilot case study: the problem
text: Writing unit tests is slow, and teams rarely know which files deserve tests first. General code assistants write tests that ignore a team’s own conventions, and nothing tells you where defects are most likely. TestPilot was our SER 594 course project at Arizona State University: generate tests that follow a team’s coding standards, and point at the files most worth testing.

title: TestPilot case study: what Yash built
text: I led the AI pipeline, the model integration and the backend. Coding standards are split into chunks, embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stored in pgvector. For each request the five closest chunks go into a structured prompt, and a local Qwen Coder 7B model, served by Ollama on a Cloud Run GPU, streams the tests back as they are written. A second pass scores each result for correctness, assertion quality, edge-case coverage and readability. Anything below 0.6 is regenerated with the critique as feedback. The defect heatmap scans a public GitHub repository with PyDriller and Radon and ranks files with a Random Forest. I trained that model and fine-tuned the generator with QLoRA on 10,000 Methods2Test pairs, keeping the training, validation and test splits separate.

title: TestPilot case study: results
text: Defect prediction. A Random Forest trained on 6,052 Java files with 21 code metrics, split 70/30, reached precision 0.39, recall 0.29, F1 0.34 and ROC-AUC 0.66. That beats chance but is not good enough to trust alone, so the heatmap is for ranking where to look first, not for deciding. Retrieval. Over 8 labelled queries against 10 standards documents, precision at 5 was 0.375 and recall at 5 was 0.94: nearly every relevant standard reaches the top five, alongside some that are not. This was measured with TF-IDF as a stand-in for pgvector.
